trivia: I have a narrow old-city lane in Kabul that is easier to find by ear than by map: finches, larks, pigeons and partridges call from rows of cages in the historic bird market.
I have Kuchi pastoralists, mobile herding communities who traditionally move with their sheep and goats between mountain pastures and warmer lowlands as the seasons change.

I have a rural tradition called ashar: when a family needs help building a mud house, harvesting wheat or clearing an irrigation canal, neighbours arrive to work without wages, knowing the favour will be returned later.
I have a reputation for generous hospitality: travellers have described being invited into village homes by people they had only just met, offered rugs to sit on and served tea or lunch.
I have saffron fields near Herat where women rise before the sun to pick purple crocus flowers, then separate the tiny red threads by hand.
I have a women-run radio station that became a classroom when girls were barred from secondary school: it broadcasts daily lessons in Dari and Pashto for students who cannot attend school.
I have a surprising use for old Korean newspapers: a visiting reporter found Korean-language dailies being used to wrap or cover food at a local restaurant.
I have a communal circle dance called Attan, in which dancers move faster and faster as the drums quicken, often finishing in a whirl of clapping and spinning.

I share the rubab, a plucked wooden instrument with a skin-covered soundboard whose deep, bright notes are heard in traditional music; UNESCO recognised its craft and performance as shared heritage across four countries in 2024.

I have a deep musical tradition, yet public music has been banned by the Taliban authorities; some taxi drivers still quietly play folk or pop songs and switch them off when morality officers approach.
I once had street photographers who used the kamra-e-faoree, a handmade wooden box that worked as both camera and darkroom, producing a black-and-white portrait in just a few minutes.
I have a traditional men's outfit called perahan tunban: a long, loose shirt worn over roomy trousers, sometimes finished with a waistcoat, turban or cap.
I have Kuchi women's dresses with very full skirts and long, wide sleeves, edged with metallic braid and decorated with amulets, pendants, tassels and tiny ornaments.
I have a long coat called a chapan, often made from striped silk and worn over a tunic and trousers; it is especially associated with the northern city of Mazar-e-Sharif.
I have Kyrgyz communities in the high Pamir where a traditional colour code marks a woman's life stage: unmarried girls may wear red veils, while married women wear white.
I have a Pashto oral-poetry form called a landay: just 22 syllables, with nine in the first line and thirteen in the second, often carrying sharp stories of love, grief, war or defiance.
I have many languages spoken across my mountain valleys and plains: alongside widely used Dari and Pashto are languages such as Uzbek, Turkmen, Balochi, Wakhi, Pashayi and Nuristani.
I welcome the spring new year in Mazar-e-Sharif with Janda Bala, a ceremony in which a huge banner is raised at a shrine as crowds gather for the start of Nowruz.
I celebrate the arrival of spring with Gol-e Surkh, the Red Tulip festival around Mazar-e-Sharif, when a normally dry landscape bursts into red flowers and celebrations can continue for weeks.
I have a spring sweet called samanak, made by slowly cooking sprouted wheat juice with flour; preparing the thick pudding can take more than two days and often becomes a communal event.

I have neighbourhood bakeries where naan is baked on the hot inner wall of a clay tandoor before dawn; in Kabul, customers have been known to start gathering at the glass bakery window around five in the morning.
I have a street snack called bolani: dough is rolled almost paper-thin, filled with potato or leek, folded over and fried until crisp on a hot iron griddle, sometimes straight from a bakery cart.
I have mantu, delicate steamed dumplings filled with seasoned minced meat and onion, usually served under tomato sauce and a thick, tangy yogurt topping.
I have a hearty noodle dish called aush, served with chickpeas or beans, yogurt, herbs and mint; it is often eaten from a bowl with a spoon big enough to feel like a small ladle.
I have chainaki, a lamb-and-chickpea stew slow-cooked for hours inside individual teapots until the meat becomes so tender it can be lifted apart with the fingers.
I have a breakfast favourite called qaymaq: the rich cream or skin that forms on simmered milk, served with fresh bread and often drizzled with honey.
I have a rice dish called Kabuli pulao, layered with tender meat, sweet carrot strips and raisins, so that a forkful can be both savoury and sweet.
I have qurut, small hard balls made by drying salted, soured yogurt or curd; they keep for a long time and can be softened into a tangy sauce or snack.
I have street sellers who stack pomegranates in bright red pyramids and press them with a hand-operated lever until a glass fills with fresh sweet-and-sour juice.
I have a horseback sport called buzkashi, in which riders battle to grab a goat or calf carcass and carry it to a scoring area while rival horsemen try to wrest it away.
I have snow leopards prowling the high mountains of the Wakhan, where they share a rugged habitat with ibex and wild sheep.
I have Marco Polo sheep, wild mountain sheep whose enormous spiral horns can stretch close to two metres from tip to tip.
I gave the world a long-haired hunting hound with a silky coat, a topknot and a ring-shaped tail; it was bred to chase gazelles and hares across rough mountain terrain.
I have wild pistachio woodlands in the north and northwest, where pistachio trees grow naturally across dry hillsides and their nuts are gathered as a valuable harvest.
I have temperate mountain forests where people gather morel mushrooms, dry their honeycomb-shaped caps and sell them into international gourmet food markets.
I have Band-e-Amir, a chain of mountain lakes with water so intensely blue it can look like bright glass set between pale cliffs.
I have a narrow strip of land called the Wakhan Corridor that reaches east to the Chinese border, with Tajikistan to the north and Pakistan to the south.
I have a place called Dragon Valley, where a ridge shaped like a dragon has two eye-like springs that send slightly salty water trickling from the rock; local goats know exactly where to find them.
I have two favourite leisure escapes near Kabul: families head to Qargha reservoir and the gardens of Paghman for picnics and a break from the city.
I have Istalif, a mountain village near Kabul known for its pottery workshops, where visitors can watch bowls and jugs take shape before they receive their distinctive blue-green glaze.
I have Mazar-e-Sharif, a city that draws large crowds for the spring banner-raising ceremony and the red-tulip celebrations around Nowruz.
I once had two giant Buddha figures carved into the cliffs of the Bamiyan Valley, one 55 metres tall and the other 38; both were destroyed in 2001, but their enormous empty niches remain.
I have the Minaret of Jam, a remote 12th-century brick tower nearly 65 metres high, covered in intricate geometric brickwork and bands of calligraphy.

I kept the Bactrian Gold safe through years of conflict: after thousands of objects were excavated from ancient tombs, museum staff hid the treasure in a bank vault, where it remained unseen until 2003.

I witnessed the disastrous retreat from Kabul in January 1842, when a British-Indian army column and its camp followers struggled through winter passes; only one European from the retreating column reached Jalalabad.
I had a Greek-founded city called Ai-Khanoum, where archaeologists uncovered the remains of a theatre, gymnasium and other buildings from the Hellenistic world.
I saw carpet designs change after the Soviet invasion of 1979: some weavers began placing tanks, helicopters and guns into patterns that had once been mostly geometric or floral.
I gained international recognition of my independence in foreign affairs through a treaty with Britain in 1919.

I had mountain communities whose pre-Islamic religion included wooden sacred figures and shrines; after a forced-conversion campaign in 1895–96, the region was renamed Nuristan, meaning 'Land of Light'.
I revealed a Bronze Age trading world when farmers near Fullol accidentally uncovered gold bowls in 1966, decorated with animals and designs linked to distant Mesopotamia.
I have an archaeological site at Mes Aynak where excavations beneath a vast copper deposit uncovered Buddhist monasteries, thousands of ancient objects and fragile manuscripts written on birch bark.

I have an underground irrigation system called karez: gently sloping tunnels carry groundwater from the foothills to fields by gravity, helping water travel across dry land without being lost to the sun.
I have Sarai Shahzada, Kabul's busy currency bazaar, where money changers and brokers use hawala networks to move payments between cities and countries without physically shipping the cash.
I changed the official taxi colour scheme in 2023: drivers in urban and suburban areas were ordered to replace the old yellow-and-white look with blue and white.
I once tested mobile-money payments for police salaries; in the pilot, officers took home about a third more after payments went directly to their phones instead of passing through intermediaries.
I am known for hand-knotted carpets and kilims, whose deep reds, dark blues and geometric patterns make them among the most recognisable keepsakes visitors look for.
I produce lapis lazuli, a deep royal-blue stone flecked with golden pyrite, which local craftspeople set into rings, beads and pendants.
I have Istalif pottery with a distinctive turquoise glaze made using ash from the root of a local ishkar plant, mixed with minerals before the pot is fired.
I have Khamak, fine white embroidery from Kandahar, often stitched onto shawls and garments; its precise geometric patterns can take months to complete.
I have richly decorated Kuchi jewellery and accessories, with dangling coins, beads, pendants and small amulets that turn clothing into a moving display of colour and sound.
